stimulus.source_note: George Washington, Farewell Address, September 17, 1796, public domain. Spelling modernized.
stimulus.text: “The great rule of conduct for us, in regard to foreign nations, is, in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible. So far as we have already formed engagements, let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop.” — George Washington, Farewell Address, September 17, 1796

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Washington's Farewell Address (1796); stem and options rewritten from fresh-written survivor original-u3-gapfill-period-end-05
stem: Historians often end Period 3 around 1800 with the election of Thomas Jefferson. Which of the following best explains why this election is a fitting endpoint for the period?

options.text: It was the first peaceful transfer of power between opposing parties, showing the republic could survive bitter partisan conflict.
It permanently abolished the Federalist Party as a political force and brought a lasting end to all partisan conflict in the young United States.
options.misconception: The Federalist Party declined but was not abolished, and partisan conflict continued.

options.text: It immediately established universal suffrage and made the United States a fully democratic nation.
options.misconception: Voting remained limited mostly to white men, with property requirements in many states.

options.text: It returned the United States to colonial status under the British Empire.
options.misconception: The election had nothing to do with Britain; the United States remained independent.

rationales.A: The election of 1800 — the “Revolution of 1800” — proved that power could change hands peacefully under the Constitution even amid fierce party hatred. Background: Jefferson tied Aaron Burr with 73 electoral votes each, and the House took thirty-six ballots to choose between them, yet the transfer still happened without violence. That demonstration that the republican experiment could endure is a natural close to the founding period.
rationales.B: The Federalist Party declined but was not abolished, and partisan conflict continued.
rationales.C: Voting remained limited mostly to white men, with property requirements in many states.
rationales.D: The election had nothing to do with Britain; the United States remained independent.
rationales.general:
1. Start with what Washington warned about. His Farewell Address feared the “spirit of party” would tear the republic apart.
2. Ask what 1800 tested. The first election in which one party took power from another — Federalists to Democratic-Republicans.
3. Ask how close it came to breaking. A tie, thirty-six ballots in the House, and open hatred between the parties — and still no violence.
4. Put it together. The republic survived its first partisan transfer, and that survival is why the period can end here.
Remember: a republic is not proven by its first election — it is proven by its first transfer of power.
